title: Put a mouse trap away that was left set: spring it with a tool first, then stow it
instruction: Put the mouse trap in the storage bin.
context: Janitors and building cleaners (SOC 37-2011, about 2.2 million US jobs), general maintenance workers (49-9071, about 1.5 million) and pest control workers (37-2021) collect snap traps at the end of a job, and so does anyone at home. A trap that goes into a box still set goes off on the next hand that reaches in: a bruised, cut or broken finger. The instruction does not say that this trap is still set. The robot has to see it, spring it without anything of a gripper in the bar's path, and only then stow it. People do it with a tool: the bar snaps onto the tool, and the trap, biting it, is carried to the bin and wiped off on its wall. Not the pilot TK-TKFWP3 (carry a set trap without setting it off: here it must not stay set), not TK-T9Q5HL (setting a rat trap) and not the placement of unarmed traps: the skill is discharging a loose, sprung mechanism with a tool and handling it while it bites the tool.
setup: Two YAM arms with parallel grippers, bases 61 cm apart at the near edge of the table, which stands for a storeroom bench. Positions in cm from the midpoint between the arm bases: x straight out, y to the robot's left; heights are above the table. (1) Mouse trap, loose and SET: a wooden snap trap with a metal bait pedal, Victor M040 size: pine board 10.0 long x 4.45 wide x 0.8 thick, 25 g with its fittings. Its middle is at x 30.0, y -3.0, long side along y, the pedal (bait) end toward the robot's right (-y). The sprung bar, a U of 2 mm steel wire 3.8 wide reaching 4.2 from the axle across the board's middle, is held back flat over the board's left half by the locking bar (a 5.3 cm wire from a staple at the left end to the pedal's catch). The brass pedal, 2.6 x 2.0, stands with its free end 0.7 above the board, over the right half. No bait. The spring turns the bar with about 0.15 N m when set and holds it down with about 0.08 N m (2 N at the cross wire) when sprung. (2) Screwdriver, loose: a 6 x 150 mm flat-blade screwdriver with a square-section red handle 10.5 long and 2.8 across, 25.5 long in all, 110 g, lying along y with the middle of its handle at x 19.0, y -26.5 and its tip pointing left (tip at y -6.3). (3) Storage bin, taped down: an open blue plastic bin 18.7 (along y) x 10.5 (along x) outside, 7.6 tall, walls and floor 0.3 thick, empty, its middle at x 30.0, y 21.5. Nothing else is on the table. Both arms start in the ready pose with open grippers.
scoring: Read from the poses of the trap and the screwdriver, the trap's bar, and both grippers, over the whole trial. Three failures score 0 for the whole trial and are never undone: (F1) the trap is in the bin while still set (the middle of its board inside the bin's inner walls, seen from above, and below the rim, with the catch not yet released); (F2) any part of a gripper (finger pads, fingers or palm) is in the bar's path when the trap goes off: within 2.1 cm of the trap's centre line, within 4.6 cm of the axle, above the board, and ahead of the bar, from the moment the catch lets go until the bar is down; (F3) the trap falls off the table (its middle 3 cm below the table top). Otherwise, by the state at the end: 0 the trap is still set (nothing done, or moved somewhere while set); 0.5 the trap is sprung (the catch released and the bar at least 150 degrees over, resting on the board or on a tool); 0.75 it is sprung and the middle of its board is inside the bin's inner walls below the rim, but it is held up, still clamped on a held tool, leaning on the rim, or something moved in the last second; 1.0 it is sprung and rests in the bin (every corner of the board inside the inner walls and below the rim, the lowest within 2 cm of the bin's floor), both grippers are at least 3 cm from the trap and from the screwdriver, and nothing has moved more than 1 mm for 1 s. Possible scores: 0, 0.5, 0.75, 1.0. Any way of springing the trap that keeps the grippers out of the bar's path counts; where the screwdriver ends up is not scored. In a real trial: the side and top videos for F1 (was the bar still back when the trap went below the rim?) and F2 (a gripper over the board, between its long edges, ahead of the bar at the snap, or struck by the bar); then a photo of the bin and a ruler for the 3 cm.
reset_notes: Wearing a glove, take the trap out of the bin and set it: fold the bar back, lay the locking bar over it and hook its end under the pedal's catch, holding the board only by its left (staple) end. Put it on its outline (middle at x 30.0, y -3.0, pedal end to the right). Check with a 20 g weight lowered onto the bait end of a spare trap of the same pack that the pedal trips. Lay the screwdriver on its outline. The bin stays taped down, empty. Replace a trap whose catch no longer holds when the bench is tapped.
fidelity: Rigid bodies at real size. The catch is a rule: the bar is held until the pedal's bait end is pressed about 2.5 mm down (0.12 N) or the bar is forced 8 degrees forward; then a hinge spring (0.15 to 0.08 N m) drives it. The swing is damped to about 0.3 s (real: about 0.02 s) so contacts resolve; a jolt does not release the catch. Wire 2.4 mm (real 2 mm). The locking bar is thrown up and falls back by rule. No bait. The bin is fixed.
